old_entry.title: Civilization
old_entry.summary: Sid Meier's Civilization is a 1991 turn-based strategy 4X video game developed and published by MicroProse.
body: Sid Meier's Civilization is a 1991 turn-based strategy 4X video game developed and published by MicroProse. The game was originally developed for MS-DOS running on a PC, and it has undergone numerous revisions for various platforms. The player is tasked with leading an entire human civilization over the course of several millennia by controlling various areas such as urban development, exploration, government, trade, research, and military. The player can control individual units and advance the exploration, conquest and settlement of the game's world. The player can also make such decisions as setting forms of government, tax rates and research priorities. The player's civilization is in competition with other computer-controlled civilizations, with which the player can enter diplomatic relationships that can either end in alliances or lead to war.

Civilization was designed by Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley following the successes of Silent Service, Sid Meier's Pirates! and Railroad Tycoon. Civilization has sold 1.5 million copies since its release and is considered one of the most influential computer games in history due to its establishment of the 4X genre. In addition to its commercial and critical success, the game has been deemed pedagogically valuable due to its presentation of historical relationships, and one of the greatest video games ever made by several publications. A multiplayer remake, Sid Meier's CivNet, was released for the PC in 1995. Civilization was followed by several sequels starting with Civilization II, with similar or modified scenarios.

old_entry.title: Metroid II: Return of Samus
old_entry.summary: Metroid II: Return of Samus is a 1991 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy.
body: Metroid II: Return of Samus is a 1991 action-adventure game developed and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy. The first Metroid game for a handheld game console, it was released in North America in November 1991 and in Japan and Europe in 1992. It follows the bounty hunter Samus Aran on her mission to eradicate the Metroids from their home planet, SR388, before the Space Pirates can obtain them. Players must find and exterminate the Metroids to progress.

Like the original Metroid, released in 1986 for the Nintendo Entertainment System, Metroid II was developed by Nintendo Research & Development 1 and produced by Gunpei Yokoi. It introduced several features that became staples of the series, including Samus's Space Jump, Spazer Beam and the Spider Ball, and round-shouldered Varia Suit.

Metroid II received positive reviews, with praise for its story, setting, and improved gameplay, but was criticized for its graphics and audio. By late 2003, it had sold 1.72 million copies worldwide. It was rereleased on the Nintendo 3DS Virtual Console service in 2011 and on the Nintendo Classics service in February 2023.

A sequel, Super Metroid, was released for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System in 1994, and a remake, Metroid: Samus Returns, was released for the Nintendo 3DS in 2017. An unofficial remake, AM2R, was released in 2016 for Windows.

old_entry.title: Lemmings
old_entry.summary: Lemmings is a 1991 puzzle and strategy video game developed by DMA Design and published by Psygnosis for the Amiga.
body: Lemmings is a 1991 puzzle and strategy video game developed by DMA Design and published by Psygnosis for the Amiga. It was later ported to numerous other platforms. The game was programmed by Russell Kay, Mike Dailly and David Jones, and was inspired by a simple animation that Dailly created while experimenting with Deluxe Paint.

The objective of the game is to guide a group of anthropomorphised lemmings through a number of obstacles to a designated exit. In any given level, the player must save a specified number or percentage of the lemmings in order to advance. To this end, the player must decide how to assign limited quantities of eight different skills to individual lemmings, allowing them to alter the landscape and/or their own behaviour so that enough of the lemmings can reach the exit safely.

Lemmings was one of the best-received video games of the early 1990s. It was the second-highest-rated game in the history of Amstrad Action, and was considered the eighth-greatest game of all time by Next Generation in 1996. Lemmings is also one of the most widely ported video games, and is estimated to have sold around 20 million copies between its various ports. The popularity of the game also led to the creation of several other Lemmings games, remakes and spin-offs, and has also inspired similar games. However, Lemmings lost considerable popularity by the late 1990s, which was attributed in part to its slow pace of gameplay compared to games of later generations.

old_entry.title: Sonic the Hedgehog
old_entry.subtitle: Speed becomes Sega’s identity
body: Sonic's shape developed alongside his movement. Naoto Ohshima recalls starting without a settled animal, while Yuji Naka wanted a character who could roll. A rabbit gave way to the hedgehog whose spines suited the attack. Planner Hirokazu Yasuhara describes repeatedly rebuilding the opening maps to balance speed against collisions with enemies. The character was therefore more than a mascot placed on top of a finished platform game. His silhouette, attack and terrain had to work together before the intended pace could become enjoyable.

Naka later recalled expecting newcomers to learn the routes carefully and accelerate on subsequent attempts. Instead, playtesters immediately ran as fast as they could. He connects that behaviour to the ring system, which lets a player carrying even one ring survive an otherwise damaging collision. The rule made room for the way people actually wanted to move. This retrospective explanation does not make every fast route effortless: learning the geography still matters, but one mistake need not end the attempt or cancel the pleasure of momentum.

A 1997 interview preserves another production decision behind Sonic's public identity. Naka describes a planned sound-test screen in which a band would perform while Sonic danced. The feature was dropped near the deadline, leaving cartridge space available. He recalls using that opportunity for the sung Sega startup sample. The familiar opening was thus connected to a discarded feature and a late allocation choice. The sung name made the company audible before the first level, using space that had been intended for another kind of performance.

On June 23, 1991 Sega launched Sonic the Hedgehog in North America and Europe. Speed is not merely a character trait: it becomes a demonstration of the Mega Drive, a way to stage scrolling, slopes and acceleration as brand identity. Yet the levels work because they alternate momentum and reading, rewarding players who learn routes, inertia and risk. The result changes Sega's public face and the rhythm of the platform game.

Development began in 1990 when Sega ordered its developers to create a game featuring a mascot for the company. The developers chose a blue hedgehog designed by Naoto Ohshima of Sega R&D9 after he won an internal character design contest, and named themselves Sonic Team to match their character. It uses a novel technique that allows Sonic's sprite to roll along curved scenery which was based on a concept by Oshima from 1989. Sonic the Hedgehog, designed for fast gameplay, was influenced by games by the Mario creator, Shigeru Miyamoto. The music was composed by Masato Nakamura, bassist of the J-pop band Dreams Come True.

Rolling downhill makes the terrain contribute to Sonic’s acceleration. Speed is therefore not only a command held down by the player; it is a relationship between a body and a curve. A well-read slope can prepare the momentum needed for an obstacle beyond the screen.

Taking damage scatters collected rings across the screen, making a mistake spectacular but sometimes recoverable. Retrieving even one can restore a margin of safety. The scramble changes the rhythm from forward momentum to a brief, urgent search around the place where everything went wrong.

editorial_features.title: Drawing a rival for Sonic
editorial_features.summary: A machine needs its own movement.
body: Sonic CD needed a visual identity that would distinguish the new disc game from its cartridge relatives. Artist Kazuyuki Hoshino recalls being fascinated by the polished, metallic appearance then associated with computer graphics. For the title animation, the team photographed a Sonic figurine with a Polaroid camera, scanned the pictures and used them as a starting point. The metallic emblem added contrast around the character. What appears to announce a new technological age also contains a practical studio procedure involving a physical object and still photographs.

Metal Sonic began with a clear relationship: an opponent who could stand beside Sonic as his double and rival. Hoshino describes imagining the red iris inside a dark eye, then designing for a direct contest between the characters. Simply repeating Sonic's movement seemed insufficient. A robot allowed another answer, and the imagined force of a drag racer's launch suggested the large booster on its back. The machine's appearance expressed a different source of speed before the race itself demonstrated what that difference could do.

In a separate 2013 interview, Hoshino explains character drawing through the actions a game requires. Sonic's spiked ball presents the protective, attacking shape used while jumping; visual design communicates an interaction rather than merely decorating it. Hoshino also distinguishes his own central intention from the feedback sought elsewhere in Sega, including Europe and marketing. That wider consultation had become more formal than in the early days. A recognizable character could emerge from a designer's proposal while still being examined by colleagues with different responsibilities.

Hoshino identifies another change when characters move from flat images into three dimensions. A two-dimensional game can repeatedly show a figure from its most effective angles. A three-dimensional model must also work from behind and from views the earlier sprite never exposed. The task is not finished by copying a familiar face. Parts that once remained unseen need decisions of their own. His explanation makes the adaptation a problem of sustained readability around a body, with the original appeal tested against a much larger range of viewpoints.

source_paragraphs: Development began in 1990 when Sega ordered its developers to create a game featuring a mascot for the company. The developers chose a blue hedgehog designed by Naoto Ohshima of Sega R&D9 after he won an internal character design contest, and named themselves Sonic Team to match their character. It uses a novel technique that allows Sonic's sprite to roll along curved scenery which was based on a concept by Oshima from 1989. Sonic the Hedgehog, designed for fast gameplay, was influenced by games by the Mario creator, Shigeru Miyamoto. The music was composed by Masato Nakamura, bassist of the J-pop band Dreams Come True.

editorial_features.title: Drawing a rival for Sonic
editorial_features.summary: A machine needs its own movement.
body: Sonic CD needed a visual identity that would distinguish the new disc game from its cartridge relatives. Artist Kazuyuki Hoshino recalls being fascinated by the polished, metallic appearance then associated with computer graphics. For the title animation, the team photographed a Sonic figurine with a Polaroid camera, scanned the pictures and used them as a starting point. The metallic emblem added contrast around the character. What appears to announce a new technological age also contains a practical studio procedure involving a physical object and still photographs.

Metal Sonic began with a clear relationship: an opponent who could stand beside Sonic as his double and rival. Hoshino describes imagining the red iris inside a dark eye, then designing for a direct contest between the characters. Simply repeating Sonic's movement seemed insufficient. A robot allowed another answer, and the imagined force of a drag racer's launch suggested the large booster on its back. The machine's appearance expressed a different source of speed before the race itself demonstrated what that difference could do.

In a separate 2013 interview, Hoshino explains character drawing through the actions a game requires. Sonic's spiked ball presents the protective, attacking shape used while jumping; visual design communicates an interaction rather than merely decorating it. Hoshino also distinguishes his own central intention from the feedback sought elsewhere in Sega, including Europe and marketing. That wider consultation had become more formal than in the early days. A recognizable character could emerge from a designer's proposal while still being examined by colleagues with different responsibilities.

Hoshino identifies another change when characters move from flat images into three dimensions. A two-dimensional game can repeatedly show a figure from its most effective angles. A three-dimensional model must also work from behind and from views the earlier sprite never exposed. The task is not finished by copying a familiar face. Parts that once remained unseen need decisions of their own. His explanation makes the adaptation a problem of sustained readability around a body, with the original appeal tested against a much larger range of viewpoints.

old_entry.title: Final Fantasy Adventure
old_entry.subtitle: Final Fantasy Adventure Brings the Action RPG into a Pocket-Sized Adventure
old_entry.summary: Ishii wanted the world to move.
body: The game released in Japan as Seiken Densetsu grew from Koichi Ishii's wish to direct an action role-playing adventure. Looking back for Mana's anniversary, he describes leaving the main Final Fantasy team's next project to take responsibility for a new experience. He wanted players to feel the fantasy world through immediate action rather than only choosing turns. The Game Boy production became Final Fantasy Adventure in North America and Mystic Quest in Europe. Those names carried a relationship to Square's existing work while the game began developing another identity.

Ishii's later account places exhilaration beside a more difficult theme: parting from someone important. He wanted the game's experience to include encounters and separation, not only the pleasure of becoming stronger. His comments about directorial responsibility connect those aims to a person making choices, rather than to an inevitable evolution of the genre. The action and story had to inhabit the same small project. A player could enjoy immediate movement while carrying a reason to care about where that movement eventually led.

The original soundtrack notes preserve several colleagues' voices. Yoshinori Kitase stresses the wish to give an action RPG narrative drama, while Kazuko Shibuya describes visual experimentation. Composer Kenji Ito identifies the game as his first complete responsibility for music and effects at Square, after contributing to SaGa 2. He thanks the other staff for ideas and Ishii for sharing his thoughts. The score was therefore part of the team's developing language, not an accompaniment simply attached once the rest of the adventure had been decided.

On June 28, 1991 Square released Seiken Densetsu for Game Boy, later known in the West as Final Fantasy Adventure and destined to become the first entry in the Mana series. Real-time combat, equipment and role-playing progression must coexist on a tiny screen with minimal controls. From that compression comes an adventure that is quick to read yet surprisingly broad, opening an independent line in Square's history.

The gameplay is similar to the original The Legend of Zelda for the NES: the world is viewed from a top-down camera angle, it is divided up into many different squares that can fit on the screen, and the main character can move up, down, left, and right across the screen. The player can interact with individuals within towns by gathering information and buying or selling items and equipment.

The main character possesses several statistics, including hit points, power, and stamina, which can all increase upon gaining an experience level. Magic spells, which expend the character's MP, can be used to heal oneself or damage enemies. These spells can only be found in certain locations or obtained from other characters at specific plot intervals. In addition, the protagonist has a power gauge that affects his attack strength—the higher the gauge, the stronger his attack will be. The speed at which it fills is directly affected by the character's will level. The gauge will slowly fill up over time, but once the main character attacks, the gauge is emptied. When the gauge is completely filled up and the main character attacks with a weapon, he will perform a special attack.

A variety of enemies can be battled on a field screen to gain experience, GP, and items. Within dungeon areas, a number of puzzles may be present and required to be solved in order for the player to advance. The player can also save at any point. A number of weapons can be found throughout the game to maneuver through obstacles such as cutting through trees and thorns.

old_entry.title: Blizzard Entertainment
old_entry.subtitle: From Three Graduates to Worlds Lived In for Decades
old_entry.summary: On February 8, 1991, Allen Adham, Michael Morhaime and Frank Pearce found Silicon & Synapse.
body: On February 8, 1991, Allen Adham, Michael Morhaime and Frank Pearce found Silicon & Synapse. Before it is called Blizzard, the studio works on ports and smaller projects, learning to read different hardware and polish games built by others. Within a few years, that technical discipline becomes a recognizable production culture: Warcraft turns strategy into serialized storytelling, Battle.net brings multiplayer into a shared service, StarCraft becomes a competitive language and World of Warcraft changes the scale of online life. Blizzard's history is also the history of how a game can stop being only a product and become a place people inhabit over time.

When Allen Adham, Michael Morhaime and Frank Pearce found Silicon & Synapse in 1991, the Blizzard name does not yet exist and neither does a major proprietary franchise. Early work includes ports for different platforms, a less glamorous activity than creating a blockbuster but an intensely educational one. Moving software across hardware forces a team to understand memory limits, controls, graphics and the behavior of someone else's code. Official retrospectives remember those years as the beginning of a culture that would later insist on polish. Before Warcraft, then, there is a technical workshop. The ability to dismantle a game, understand why it works and rebuild it elsewhere prepares the studio to design its own systems with the same attention to detail.

Warcraft: Orcs & Humans in 1994 offers two campaigns, Humans and Orcs, and places real-time competition at the center of the studio's identity. Blizzard now presents it as the beginning of the Warcraft saga, but the decisive shift is already visible in the way system and fiction support one another. Gathering resources, building bases and producing units are not abstract actions: they belong to two factions that players learn to recognize through voices, architecture and roles. Strategy becomes a repeatable storytelling vehicle. Every match teaches rules, every campaign adds context, and multiplayer proves that the world can continue beyond the authored story. It is the model that will make decades of expansion for Azeroth possible.

With Diablo, Battle.net becomes part of the Blizzard experience in 1996. The novelty is not merely allowing an online match, but reducing the distance between owning a game and finding other people to play it with. Accounts, chat, game creation and player discovery enter a shared environment that Blizzard will continue to expand. This also changes the relationship between studio and audience: software no longer ends when a disc is printed, because the network makes communities, problems and play habits visible. Battle.net therefore becomes a cultural infrastructure as well as a technical one. By the time StarCraft and later World of Warcraft arrive, the studio has already learned that connection, identity and continuity can be parts of game design.
